methods.name: on_control_permission_request
methods.doc:
Ask the user whether something may control the app.

'Control' is deliberately broad: running commands, reading
this app's log, and whatever that grows into. Answer via
``on_result``, which may be called later (from a dialog) or
immediately (from policy).

The default answers ``CANNOT_ASK``, which is the honest
answer for a mode with no way to prompt -- the request is
then held and re-put once a mode that can ask activates.
An app-mode with a UI should override this; one running
without a user present (a dedicated server) should answer
``ALLOW``, since nobody is there to ask and the operator
already owns the account.

methods.name: get_default_type_id
methods.doc:
Return a type-id to be assumed when none is present.

By default, dataclassio errors when deserializing multitype
data that contains no type-id value. Overriding this to return
a type-id changes that behavior: data with no type-id present
will be deserialized as the returned type, and instances of
that type will be serialized *without* a type-id value. This
both saves a bit of space and allows 'upgrading' an existing
regular dataclass to a multitype - simply designate the
original dataclass type as the default and old serialized data
will remain loadable (and data for the default type will remain
loadable by old code).

Be aware of the following, however:

- Once serialized data exists anywhere without type-id values,
  the default type-id must never be changed or removed; doing
  so would cause that existing data to be silently
  reinterpreted as some other type (or to error).
- A missing type-id normally acts as a sanity check when
  deserializing; defining a default effectively disables that
  check, meaning malformed data may deserialize successfully
  as the default type instead of erroring.

methods.name: get_fixed_profiles
methods.doc:
Return the only profiles this session's lobby offers, if any.

None (the default) offers each player their own profiles, with
the usual choice of a random one and (locally) of editing
them. A session made to show particular characters can return
those instead: each a character's json as a cloud profile's
arrives (name, icon and spaz parts, and optionally the profile
name it goes by). Every player is then offered exactly those
and nothing else -- no random entry, and no editing unless
:meth:`can_edit_fixed_profiles` says so -- and what they pick
isn't remembered as their usual profile.

base class's ``__init__``, before a subclass's own has
returned), and again whenever the lobby reloads profiles
(send the session a
:class:`~bascenev1.PlayerProfilesChangedMessage` after
changing what this returns).

classes.name: Depiction
classes.doc:
Depiction(json: str)

A depiction registered in a scene, for nodes to show.

Built from a json-serialized :class:`bacommon.depiction.Depiction`
(a name, a character's icon, ...) and assigned to node attrs of
the depiction type (a ``depictiondisplay`` node's ``depiction``,
say). It crosses the stream once however many nodes show it;
every machine draws it natively, as a placeholder if it can't.

Lifetime works like :class:`Material`: the depiction lives as
long as something references it (this object or a node attr)
and leaves the session automatically once nothing does.

Must be created in a host activity or host session context, and
can only be assigned to nodes of that same scene (scene objects
never cross scenes; the session's lobby has its own). To show
the same thing in another activity, build another from the same
json there.

methods.name: as_integer_ratio

Return a pair of integers, whose ratio is equal to the original int.

The ratio is in lowest terms and has a positive denominator.

>>> (10).as_integer_ratio()

>>> (-10).as_integer_ratio()

>>> bin(13)

methods.name: conjugate

methods.name: from_bytes
methods.doc:
Return the integer represented by the given array of bytes.

  bytes
    Holds the array of bytes to convert.  The argument must either
    support the buffer protocol or be an iterable object producing bytes.
    Bytes and bytearray are examples of built-in objects that support the
    buffer protocol.
  byteorder
    The byte order used to represent the integer.  If byteorder is 'big',
    the most significant byte is at the beginning of the byte array.  If
    byteorder is 'little', the most significant byte is at the end of the
    byte array.  To request the native byte order of the host system, use
    sys.byteorder as the byte order value.  Default is to use 'big'.
  signed
    Indicates whether two's complement is used to represent the integer.

methods.name: is_integer
methods.doc: Returns True. Exists for duck type compatibility with float.is_integer.

methods.name: to_bytes
methods.doc:
Return an array of bytes representing an integer.

  length
    Length of bytes object to use.  An OverflowError is raised if the
    integer is not representable with the given number of bytes.  Default
    is length 1.
  byteorder
    The byte order used to represent the integer.  If byteorder is 'big',
    the most significant byte is at the beginning of the byte array.  If
    byteorder is 'little', the most significant byte is at the end of the
    byte array.  To request the native byte order of the host system, use
    sys.byteorder as the byte order value.  Default is to use 'big'.
  signed
    Determines whether two's complement is used to represent the integer.
    If signed is False and a negative integer is given, an OverflowError
    is raised.

classes.name: LangStr
classes.doc:
LangStr(json: str, packages: Sequence[int] | None = None,
        wrap: tuple[int, int | None, int | None] | None = None)

A deferred, language-agnostic complex string (native).

The verified-local counterpart of
:class:`bacommon.langstr.LangStrSpec` (see the D28 semantic
split -- holding one of these implies displayability here):
holds tokens, not text, and evaluates to a flat string in the
client's locale at display time. Construct from the canonical
wire JSON of any language-string form; pass the payload's
``packages`` manifest to bind integer-indexed values at parse,
and optionally a ``wrap`` triple (min-lines, max-lines,
max-chars-per-line; None = unlimited) as a usage-site override
of the string's definition-time line-wrapping. Immutable, with
content equality and hashing. Accepted anywhere
``str | babase.Lstr`` is accepted for display.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.doc:
evaluate(*, wrap: bool = True) -> str

Evaluate to flat display text in the client's locale.

Fail-visible: structural problems yield a ``LANGSTR_ERROR:...``
sentinel string (with a logged warning) rather than raising.

Pass ``wrap=False`` to skip the string's line-wrapping hints
(for code wrapping the text itself); newlines in the text are
kept either way.

methods.name: evaluate_timed
methods.doc:
evaluate_timed(*, wrap: bool = True) -> tuple[str, float | None]

Evaluate, also returning how soon the text changes.

Returns the text :meth:`evaluate` would (``wrap`` works the
same), plus the seconds until
it would next read differently -- a number only for time-varying
strings (those holding a moment, such as a countdown), else
``None``. Widgets showing a language-string handle this
themselves; this is for code displaying the text some other
way, which can re-evaluate when that time comes.

methods.name: from_text
methods.doc:
from_text(text: str) -> babase.LangStr

Wrap a plain string as a literal language-string.

The text is shown exactly as given in every locale -- any
``{`` or ``}`` displays literally, with no substitution. Use
this to pass a piece of already-final text (a name a mod
supplied, a value with no translation entry) through an API
that wants a :class:`~babase.LangStr`. Anything that needs
substitutions or translation should be an authored
asset-package entry instead, so its arguments are type-checked.

methods.name: join
methods.doc:
join(items: Sequence[babase.LangStr], separator: str = '') -> babase.LangStr

Combine language-strings into one, shown one after another.

``separator`` is literal text placed between items (a newline
for a list, say); its braces display literally. Each item keeps
its own translation and arguments, so a variable-length list
of authored entries (one line per player, ...) stays fully
localized. Items must be language-strings -- wrap plain text
with :meth:`from_text`. Raises ValueError for more than 256
items or a result nested too deeply.

Server code (or anything without a native language-string) can
build the same thing in spec form with
:meth:`bacommon.langstr.LangStrSpecValue.join`.

classes.name: LocalDisplay
classes.doc:
The local side of a ``localdisplay`` scene node.

Each machine receiving the node (host and every client) gets its
own one of these, owning a private context whose scene is never
streamed anywhere. Actors created within that context bind to the
display exactly as they would to an activity, and are expired when
the node dies.

Only display-style actors make sense here (text, images,
animation). Anything that reaches for players, shared objects or
materials belongs to an activity and will not work in a display.

Instances are created by the engine; don't instantiate these
directly.

classes.name: LocalDisplayConfig
classes.doc:
Describes what a :class:`LocalDisplay` should show.

Configs ride the ``config`` attr of a ``localdisplay`` scene node
wrapped in a :class:`LocalDisplayConfigSet`; every machine that
receives the node (the host included) picks the entry for its own
build and builds its own local version of what it describes.

Forward compatibility: configs are decoded lossily, so a client
that predates a config *type* gets :class:`UnknownLocalDisplayConfig`
(which the set's selection skips over in favor of an older entry,
or shows nothing), and one that predates a *field* on a known type
ignores it while its own defaults fill any fields the newer host
omitted. New types and fields are therefore safe to add at any
time; only removing or retyping an existing field is a breaking
change.

methods.name: get_default_type_id
methods.doc:
Return a type-id to be assumed when none is present.

By default, dataclassio errors when deserializing multitype
data that contains no type-id value. Overriding this to return
a type-id changes that behavior: data with no type-id present
will be deserialized as the returned type, and instances of
that type will be serialized *without* a type-id value. This
both saves a bit of space and allows 'upgrading' an existing
regular dataclass to a multitype - simply designate the
original dataclass type as the default and old serialized data
will remain loadable (and data for the default type will remain
loadable by old code).

Be aware of the following, however:

- Once serialized data exists anywhere without type-id values,
  the default type-id must never be changed or removed; doing
  so would cause that existing data to be silently
  reinterpreted as some other type (or to error).
- A missing type-id normally acts as a sanity check when
  deserializing; defining a default effectively disables that
  check, meaning malformed data may deserialize successfully
  as the default type instead of erroring.

methods.name: get_type
methods.doc: Return the subclass for each of our type-ids.

methods.name: get_type_cached
methods.doc:
Version of :meth:`get_type()` with caching.

Generally end-users of a multi-type class should use this
instead of calling :meth:`get_type()` directly. It lazily caches
looked up types so can be significantly more efficient with
large multitypes and repeat lookups.

methods.name: get_type_id_type
methods.doc: Return the Enum type this class uses as its type-id.

classes.name: LocalDisplayConfigSet
classes.doc:
What a ``localdisplay`` node's ``config`` attr actually carries.

A map of minimum engine build number to the
:class:`LocalDisplayConfig` clients at or above that build should
use. Each client picks the entry with the highest build it
satisfies, so a host can hand newer clients a richer display while
older ones keep getting something they understand. A single entry
at build 0 applies to everyone (see :meth:`single`).

methods.name: select
methods.doc:
Return the config for a given engine build, or None.

Entries requiring newer builds are skipped, as are entries that
decoded to :class:`UnknownLocalDisplayConfig` when an older
recognized entry is available.

methods.name: single
methods.doc: Return a set holding one config that applies to all builds.

methods.name: to_json
methods.doc: Return our json form for a node's ``config`` attr.

classes.name: LocalDisplayHandler
classes.doc:
Builds and manages the content of one :class:`LocalDisplay`.

One of these exists per display; it is created via the factory
registered for the display's config type (see
:func:`register_local_display_handler`) with the display's context
current, so it can create actors, nodes, timers, etc. directly.
Everything it creates dies with the display.

methods.name: on_config_changed
methods.doc:
Called when the config changes but keeps its type.

The default implementation ignores the change.

methods.name: on_expire
methods.doc:
Called when the display is expiring.

Actors and nodes created under the display are torn down
automatically after this; only clean up things that aren't.

methods.name: on_visible_changed
methods.doc:
Called when the node's ``visible`` attr changes.

Hosts flip this off ahead of deleting the node so displays get
a chance to fade out gracefully.

classes.name: LocalDisplayTypeID
classes.doc: Type ID for each of our :class:`LocalDisplayConfig` subclasses.

methods.name: from_spec

Loadable handle for a spec that arrived from outside.

Server-sent content and the wire carry plain specs; this is how

Verification still happens in :meth:`get`.

methods.doc: Resolve and return the live scene mesh for this reference.

methods.name: ui
methods.doc:
This same verified reference, in ui form.

Both featuresets' handles assert the same thing -- the
package was construct-mode-resolved -- so converting between
them preserves that guarantee; only what :meth:`get` loads
differs (a ui mesh vs a scene-bound one). Use at a ui boundary
consuming scene-authored config, such as a spaz appearance's
icon.

There is deliberately no reverse ``scene()`` on the ui types:
``scene_v1`` always pulls in ``ui_v1`` (via ``classic``), but a
spinoff may include ``ui_v1`` with no ``scene_v1`` at all.

methods.name: allows_tutorial
methods.doc:
Return whether this session may open with the tutorial.

A player who hasn't seen the tutorial gets it at the start of
their first session; a session that isn't a first game in that
sense can say no here. (Asked during setup, as
:meth:`get_fixed_playlist` is.)

methods.name: can_edit_fixed_profiles
methods.doc:
Return whether the lobby offers editing its fixed profiles.

Only asked of a session with fixed profiles (see
:meth:`get_fixed_profiles`). If so, local players get the
lobby's usual edit entry, and choosing it calls
:meth:`edit_fixed_profiles` instead of opening their own
profiles. Asked whenever the fixed profiles are.

methods.name: edit_fixed_profiles
methods.doc:
Open whatever edits the lobby's fixed profiles.

Called (with no context set) when a local player chooses the
lobby's edit entry in a session where
:meth:`can_edit_fixed_profiles` is True. Whatever opens
should end by changing what :meth:`get_fixed_profiles` returns
and telling the session so (see there).

methods.name: get_fixed_playlist
methods.doc:
Return the playlist this session always plays, if it has one.

None (the default) plays whichever playlist the player has
chosen in their config. A subclass made for one purpose (a
session that exists to show one game, say) can return its own:
entries as a config playlist holds them, a ``type`` and
``settings`` each. It is asked while the session is being set
up, before its own ``__init__`` has returned.

methods.name: get_fixed_profiles

Return the only profiles this session's lobby offers, if any.

None (the default) offers each player their own profiles, with
the usual choice of a random one and (locally) of editing
them. A session made to show particular characters can return
those instead: each a character's json as a cloud profile's
arrives (name, icon and spaz parts, and optionally the profile
name it goes by). Every player is then offered exactly those
and nothing else -- no random entry, and no editing unless
:meth:`can_edit_fixed_profiles` says so -- and what they pick
isn't remembered as their usual profile.

Asked as the session's lobby is made (which is during the
base class's ``__init__``, before a subclass's own has
returned), and again whenever the lobby reloads profiles
(send the session a
:class:`~bascenev1.PlayerProfilesChangedMessage` after
changing what this returns).

methods.name: on_app_mode_config
methods.doc:
Called when an app-mode is about to become active.

``config`` is the :class:`~babase.AppModeConfig` the incoming
mode built to describe how it should run; its concrete type
identifies the mode, so a plugin targeting a particular mode
checks for that mode's config type and amends what it finds::

    @override
    def on_app_mode_config(
        self, config: babase.AppModeConfig
    ) -> None:
        if isinstance(config, baclassic.ClassicAppModeConfig):
            config.ui_assets.trophy = my_trophy_texture

By convention, only *describe* here -- mutate the config and
touch nothing live. The mode reads the final result as it
activates, so if several plugins amend the same value the last
writer wins.

Only the config is passed, not the mode itself; that is
deliberate, to keep plugins amending the description rather
than reaching into a mode that is not active yet.

This never fires before construct-mode completes (plugins do
not run at all until then), so assets are safe to load here.

doc.__changed_from__: Called when the app reaches the running state.
doc.__modified_value__:
Called when the app reaches the running state.

Specifically, this fires once boot-time asset-package bring-up
has completed but before the launch intent is dispatched to an
app-mode. That means every asset-package the meta-scan found a
``# ba_meta require asset-package`` line for (including your
own) is resolved and safe to load by this point, while it is
still early enough to influence what the app does next --
setting :attr:`~babase.App.mode_selector`, registering app
subsystems, or driving an intent of your own via
:meth:`~babase.App.set_intent()`.

Note that a plugin's module is not even imported until this
point, so plugin code never runs before assets are ready.

classes.name: Quat
classes.doc:
A quaternion representing a rotation in 3d space.

These can be created the following ways (checked in this order):
 - With no args, the identity (no-op) rotation is created.
 - With a four-member sequence arg, sequence values are copied.
 - Otherwise assumes individual w/x/y/z args (positional or keywords).

Quats are immutable, and are accepted anywhere a four-float
sequence is, so one can be assigned directly to node attrs such as
:attr:`bascenev1.Node.rotate`.

Note that most rotations are more easily built using
:meth:`~bascenev1.Quat.from_angles()` than by passing raw values
here.

Attributes:
   w (float):
      The quaternion's real component.

   x (float):
      The quaternion's X component.

   y (float):
      The quaternion's Y component.

   z (float):
      The quaternion's Z component.

methods.name: from_angles
methods.doc:
from_angles(heading: float = 0.0, pitch: float = 0.0, roll: float = 0.0) -> Quat

Create a rotation from Euler angles, in degrees.

Heading is a rotation about the up (y) axis, pitch about the
sideways (x) axis, and roll about the forward (z) axis. They are
applied in that order, each about the axes left by the previous
one, so pitch tips an object relative to wherever its heading
left it facing.

Signs follow the usual aircraft convention: positive heading
turns right, positive pitch aims up, and positive roll banks
right.

methods.name: from_direction
methods.doc:
from_direction(direction: Sequence[float], up: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) -> Quat

Create a rotation aiming forward (+z) along a direction.

The up vector is only a hint for which way to roll about that
direction; it gets squared up against it rather than being
followed exactly, so passing a rough one is fine. Aiming straight
along up leaves the roll undefined, in which case an arbitrary
one is picked rather than failing.

methods.name: inverse
methods.doc:
inverse() -> Quat

Return the rotation undoing this one.

methods.name: normalized
methods.doc:
normalized() -> Quat

Return a unit-length version of this rotation.

Composing many rotations together can accumulate enough error to
visibly skew things; this cleans that up.

methods.name: slerp
methods.doc:
slerp(from_quat: Quat, to_quat: Quat, amount: float) -> Quat

Interpolate between two rotations along the shortest arc.

An amount of 0 returns the first rotation and 1 the second, with
values between sweeping smoothly from one to the other at a
constant rate. Note that interpolating a rotation's individual
values (as :func:`bascenev1.animate_array()` would) does not do
this correctly, so prefer this call when animating rotations.

:attr:`~babase.AppState.LOADING` state.

Called just after an app-mode becomes the active one.

the mode is fully in place by the time this runs. Useful for
work that needs *some* app-mode present but doesn't care
which -- e.g. re-putting a question that no earlier mode was
able to ask.

classes.name: SceneV1AssetSet
classes.doc:
The assets the scene_v1 node layer draws itself with.

An app-mode using scene_v1 carries one of these on its
app-mode config and hands it to
:func:`bascenev1.set_scene_asset_set` when activating,
which is what lets an app-mode (or a plugin amending its
config) reskin the art scene_v1 nodes draw themselves
with.

Slots hold asset *handles*, not loaded assets; nothing
loads until the set is applied at activation, so art that
gets replaced is never loaded at all. Every slot defaults
to scene_v1's own art, so a bare ``SceneV1AssetSet()`` is
complete and a supplier names only what it changes.

classes.name: SceneViewer
classes.doc:
SceneViewer(width: int, height: int)

A self-contained scene drawn to a texture, for showing in ui.

The scene is this machine's alone and wholly separate from any
game going on: it has its own nodes, look, camera, and clock,
and makes no sound. Build what should be in it by creating
nodes, materials, and so on under its :attr:`context`, and show
it by handing its :attr:`source` to a viewer widget (or by
drawing its :attr:`texture` some other way). It runs only while
its picture is being drawn somewhere and stands still otherwise.

Size is in pixels. A viewer widget sets it to the size it shows
the picture at, so what is passed here matters only until then
(or when drawing the texture some other way).

The viewer lives as long as this object does.

:meta private:

methods.name: set_camera
methods.doc:
set_camera(position: Sequence[float], target: Sequence[float],
  field_of_view: float = 30.0, near_clip: float = 1.0,
  far_clip: float = 100.0,
  min_horizontal_field_of_view: float = 0.0) -> None

Set where the scene is seen from and what is looked at.

Field of view is vertical, in degrees, so what is looked at
takes up the same share of the picture's height whatever
shape the picture is. A picture narrow enough to see less
across than min_horizontal_field_of_view (if one is given)
sees that much across and more up and down instead, so that
what is looked at gets smaller rather than cut off at the
sides.

Nothing nearer than near_clip or farther than far_clip gets
drawn; keep the span between them no wider than the scene
needs.

methods.name: set_camera_shake
methods.doc:
set_camera_shake(strength: float, stiffness: float = 30.0,
  damping: float = 2.0, poke_interval_min: float = 0.5,
  poke_interval_max: float = 1.0) -> None

Give the camera a hand-held shake.

The camera stays where it is, but its aim wobbles left/right
and up/down on a damped spring, kicked in a random direction
every so often (a random time between the two poke intervals,
in seconds, apart). Strength is the size of a kick in degrees
per second of spin; 0 turns shake off. Stiffness and damping
shape the spring: stiffer wobbles faster, more damping settles
sooner. Still while camera shake is disabled.

methods.name: set_camera_tilt_orbit
methods.doc:
set_camera_tilt_orbit(amount: float) -> None

Swing the camera around its target as the device turns.

On devices with a gyro, turning the device turns the view of
what the camera looks at with it, the camera keeping its
distance and aim. Amount scales the turn: 1.0 turns the camera
as far as the device turned, 0.0 (the default) not at all. The
turn eases back to center over a couple of seconds once the
device holds still. Nothing happens while camera gyro is
disabled.

methods.name: set_depth_of_field
methods.doc:
set_depth_of_field(focus: tuple[float, float] | None,
  blur: tuple[float, float] | None = None) -> None

Set what of the scene is in focus.

Both are pairs of distances out from the camera along the way
it is looking, nearer one first. Everything between the two
focus distances is sharp; from there things get blurrier out
to the blur distances (which lie outside the focus ones),
past which they are as blurry as things get. Pass None for
focus to have everything in focus, which is how viewers
start out.

This shows only where graphics quality is high or better;
below that everything is sharp regardless.

methods.name: set_size
methods.doc:
set_size(width: int, height: int) -> None

Set the size of our texture in pixels.

methods.name: set_sound
methods.doc:
set_sound(enabled: bool, volume: float = 1.0,
  pan_scale: float = 1.0) -> None

Let the scene make sound (viewers start out silent).

Sounds are heard as the viewer's camera would hear them, not
the game's: placed relative to it (its steady aim; shake is
left out), their gain scaled by volume, and how far to the
sides they sit scaled by pan_scale (more pans them wider).

methods.name: shutdown
methods.doc:
shutdown() -> None

Take the scene down for good.

Everything in it is destroyed and most calls on this object
raise from here on. Happens by itself when this object goes
away; call it to not depend on when that is.

arrives (name, icon and spaz parts, and optionally the profile
name it goes by). Every player is then offered exactly those
and nothing else -- no random entry, and no editing unless

Asked as the session's lobby is made (which is during the

methods.name: get_icon_depiction
methods.doc:
get_icon_depiction() -> bascenev1.Depiction | None

Return the player's icon as a depiction, if they have one.

Players on cloud profiles have one (the icon composed with
their profile); anyone else (legacy profiles, random looks,
bots) gets None and should be shown via :meth:`get_icon`. Show it
with a ``depictiondisplay`` node or anything else accepting a
:class:`~bascenev1.Depiction` (the
:class:`~bascenev1lib.actor.image.Image` actor,
:func:`~bascenev1.broadcastmessage` images). The usual pattern is
``player.get_icon_depiction() or player.get_icon()``.

The depiction is made in the current context's scene (scene
objects never cross scenes), so ask in the context it will be
shown in rather than holding one across activities.

Return the json :meth:`get_icon_depiction` builds from, if any.

stats record, say).

methods.doc:
get_name_depiction() -> bascenev1.Depiction | None

Return the player's name as a depiction, if they have one.

This is the name as it shows on its own (an account's capsule, a
global profile's icon, or plain text), for places such as score
screens; players who joined through the lobby have one. It
carries the player's color (their team's in team games). Names
worked into other text should stay :meth:`getname`. Show it with
a ``depictiondisplay`` node or the
:class:`~bascenev1lib.actor.text.Text` actor. The usual pattern is
``player.get_name_depiction() or player.getname(full=True)``.

The depiction is made in the current context's scene (scene
objects never cross scenes), so ask in the context it will be
shown in rather than holding one across activities.

methods.doc:
send_feedback(*, event: str = 'impact_received') -> None

Request physical feedback (controller rumble, device vibration) for
whoever is controlling this player.

``event`` says what happened, not what it should feel like; each
platform renders it however it does that best. Valid values are
'join', 'collect', 'grab', 'impact_dealt', 'impact_received' and
'death'. Note a device may render nothing at all for an event its
hardware cannot represent well, so don't rely on any particular one
always being felt.

Does nothing if the player has already left the game.

doc.__changed_from__:
play(volume: float = 1.0, position: Sequence[float] | None = None,
     host_only: bool = False) -> None

Play the sound a single time.

If position is not provided, the sound will be at a constant volume
everywhere. Position should be a float tuple of size 3.
doc.__modified_value__:
play(volume: float = 1.0, position: Sequence[float] | None = None,
     host_only: bool = False, play_group: str | None = None,
     play_group_cap: int | None = None,
     priority: bascenev1.SoundPriority | None = None) -> None

Play the sound a single time.

If position is not provided, the sound will be at a constant volume
everywhere. Position should be a float tuple of size 3.

Only so many sounds can play at once, and the last three arguments
bear on which ones do when there are more than that. Sounds
belong to play groups; by default a sound's group comes from its
name, with numbered variations of a sound ('explosion01',
'explosion02') sharing one. Only a few sounds of a group play at
once, a new one cutting off the group's oldest. Pass
``play_group`` to count this play toward a group of your choosing
and ``play_group_cap`` to change how many of that group may play
at once (1 means each play cuts off the last). ``priority``
overrides the sound's own; see
:class:`~bascenev1.SoundPriority`.

classes.name: SoundHandle
classes.doc: A sound reference that can also load the live scene sound.

methods.name: from_spec
methods.doc:
Loadable handle for a spec that arrived from outside.

Server-sent content and the wire carry plain specs; this is how
one becomes loadable without anyone rebuilding a path string.
Verification still happens in :meth:`get`.

methods.name: get
methods.doc: Resolve and return the live scene sound for this reference.

methods.name: ui
methods.doc:
This same verified reference, in ui form.

Both featuresets' handles assert the same thing -- the
package was construct-mode-resolved -- so converting between
them preserves that guarantee; only what :meth:`get` loads
differs (a ui sound vs a scene-bound one). Use at a ui boundary
consuming scene-authored config, such as a spaz appearance's
icon.

There is deliberately no reverse ``scene()`` on the ui types:
``scene_v1`` always pulls in ``ui_v1`` (via ``classic``), but a
spinoff may include ``ui_v1`` with no ``scene_v1`` at all.

classes.name: SoundPriority
classes.doc:
How much a sound matters when more sounds want to play than can at
once. When everything is busy, a new sound takes the place of the
oldest playing sound of the lowest priority at or below its own
(sounds that loop are never cut off this way).

Sounds are 'default' unless their asset says otherwise.

classes.name: SpazDef
classes.doc:
SpazDef(json: str)

A spaz definition: how a spaz node looks, sounds, and is
proportioned.

Built from a json spaz definition (a character's spaz part, as
delivered by the master server for a player's verified profile
or bundled for the builtin characters; see
:func:`bascenev1.split_character`) and assigned to a spaz node's
``spaz_def`` attr. The definition is opaque here; the node draws,
voices, and proportions itself from it, wearing a standard-spaz
standin until any media it references is available locally.

Lifetime works like :class:`Material`: the definition lives as
long as something references it (this object or a node attr)
and leaves the session automatically once nothing does.

Must be created in a host activity or host session context, and
can only be assigned to nodes of that same scene (scene objects
never cross scenes). A player's cloud look is made per scene for
you: read ``SessionPlayer.cloud_spaz_def`` in the context it
will be used in.

This same verified reference, in ui form.

Both featuresets' handles assert the same thing -- the
package was construct-mode-resolved -- so converting between
them preserves that guarantee; only what :meth:`get` loads
differs (a ui texture vs a scene-bound one). Use at a ui boundary

methods.name: get_default_type_id
methods.doc:
Return a type-id to be assumed when none is present.

By default, dataclassio errors when deserializing multitype
data that contains no type-id value. Overriding this to return
a type-id changes that behavior: data with no type-id present
will be deserialized as the returned type, and instances of
that type will be serialized *without* a type-id value. This
both saves a bit of space and allows 'upgrading' an existing
regular dataclass to a multitype - simply designate the
original dataclass type as the default and old serialized data
will remain loadable (and data for the default type will remain
loadable by old code).

Be aware of the following, however:

- Once serialized data exists anywhere without type-id values,
  the default type-id must never be changed or removed; doing
  so would cause that existing data to be silently
  reinterpreted as some other type (or to error).
- A missing type-id normally acts as a sanity check when
  deserializing; defining a default effectively disables that
  check, meaning malformed data may deserialize successfully
  as the default type instead of erroring.

methods.name: get_type_cached

Version of :meth:`get_type()` with caching.

Generally end-users of a multi-type class should use this
instead of calling :meth:`get_type()` directly. It lazily caches
looked up types so can be significantly more efficient with
large multitypes and repeat lookups.

doc.__changed_from__:
Wrap a callable and arguments into a single callable object.

When passed a bound method as the callable, the instance portion of
it is weak-referenced, meaning the underlying instance is free to
die if all other references to it go away. Should this occur,
calling the weak-call is simply a no-op.

Think of this as a handy way to tell an object to do something at
some point in the future if it happens to still exist.

**EXAMPLE A:** This code will create a ``FooClass`` instance and
call its ``bar()`` method 5 seconds later; it will be kept alive
even though we overwrite its variable with None because the bound
method we pass as a timer callback (``foo.bar``) strong-references
it::

    foo = FooClass()
    babase.apptimer(5.0, foo.bar)
    foo = None

**EXAMPLE B:** This code will *not* keep our object alive; it will
die when we overwrite it with ``None`` and the timer will be a no-op
when it fires::

    foo = FooClass()
    babase.apptimer(5.0, ba.WeakCall(foo.bar))
    foo = None

**EXAMPLE C:** Wrap a method call with some positional and keyword
args::

    myweakcall = babase.WeakCall(self.dostuff, argval1,
                                 namedarg=argval2)

    # Now we have a single callable to run that whole mess.
    # The same as calling myobj.dostuff(argval1, namedarg=argval2)
    # (provided my_obj still exists; this will do nothing otherwise).
    myweakcall()

Note: additional args and keywords you provide to the weak-call
constructor are stored as regular stron

get_auto_screen_inset_amount() -> float

Return the screen-inset amount automatic mode uses here.

Screen insets pull the virtual bounds in from the screen edges,
from 0 (only what the OS reports as obscured) to 1 (the max
margins). With the ``Screen Insets`` config value at ``Auto``, the
amount comes from context (TV or not, ui scale); this returns
that value. With it at ``Custom``, ``Custom Screen Insets`` is
used instead.

functions.name: get_depiction_control
functions.doc:
get_depiction_control(widget: bauiv1.Widget) -> bauiv1.Viewer | None

Get the object for driving an image's or button's depiction.

Some depictions have a live object behind them whose methods adjust
what is shown locally, without a new depiction from the server --
a live character viewer is its :class:`bauiv1.Viewer`, for
instance (a slider could recolor its character as it moves).
Returns None for depictions offering nothing (or not yet shown;
live objects are made the first time a depiction is drawn). What
is shown remains the server's to decide: the next depiction it
sends replaces local tweaks. Don't hold the object long; a
depiction can be replaced at any time.

This is the legacy ``langdata.json`` payload (translated language

asset-package's flavor-invariant ``constant`` bucket (logical path
``legacylangdata``) rather than a bundled data file.

Returns ``{}`` when the blob is unavailable (headless / no bundled
asset-package manifest / not yet resolved) or on any read error, so
callers can ``.get(...)`` safely.

get_virtual_outer_rect() -> tuple[float, float, float, float]

Return the full visible drawing area in virtual coords.

Returns the left, bottom, right, and top edges of the active render
rect expressed in virtual coordinates. This equals (0, 0, virtual-
res-x, virtual-res-y) unless the virtual bounds are inset to dodge
camera cutouts or the like, in which case left/bottom may be
negative and right/top may exceed the virtual res. Use this to
extend visuals to the edge of the visible area; note that content
outside the regular virtual bounds may be partially obscured.

functions.name: logic_thread_submit
functions.doc:
Run a call on the logic thread from another thread; get a future.

The logic-thread counterpart of
:meth:`concurrent.futures.Executor.submit()`, with the same
type-checked argument passing. Use it from background threads for
the bits of work that must happen on the logic thread (reading app
state, querying input devices, etc.) while the rest stays off it.

The call runs with no context set (as with
``pushcall(from_other_thread=True)``), so UI calls are fine to make
from it. Its return value or exception lands on the returned
future; nothing is logged, so an exception is lost if nobody
checks. Cancelling the future before the call starts skips the
call.

Blocking on the result is the usual pattern, so pass a timeout to
:meth:`~concurrent.futures.Future.result()` unless you know the
logic thread will get to it; late in app shutdown it may never run.

Must not be called from the logic thread itself: blocking there on
the result would deadlock it. Just make the call directly (or use
:func:`~babase.pushcall()` to defer it).

functions.name: set_ui_asset_set
functions.doc:
Supply the assets the ui_v1 widget layer draws itself with.

Called by an app-mode during activation (normally from
:meth:`~babase.AppMode.on_activate`, with the
:class:`UIAssetSet` carried by its app-mode config), before
asking the native layer to activate the mode -- ui_v1 reads
the set as it builds its widgets. Calling more than once is
fine: the last call before an activation is the one that
takes effect. Note that a call made while ui_v1 is already
active does not restyle the live ui; it applies at the next
activation (which happens on every session change).

The supplied art is wiped by ui_v1's app-subsystem
:meth:`~babase.AppSubsystem.reset` at every app-mode switch,
so a mode can never inherit a previous mode's art. A
ui-using mode that never supplies its own gets a disabled
('zombie') ui and a logged error rather than a crash.

functions.name: snap_slider_value
functions.doc:
A :func:`bauiv1.sliderwidget` value, cleaned up for storing.

The widget works in single precision and snaps to its increment
grid in that arithmetic, so it reports things like
``0.800000011920929`` for the ``0.8`` a user picked. This returns
the value at the same grid point in the decimal form the user
would write, clamped to the range -- what config files and page
state should hold. Every consumer of slider values goes through
here so they agree on it.

An ``increment`` of zero or less means no grid; the value is
only clamped.

functions.name: translate_server_text
functions.doc:
Translate legacy-server-sent English text for display.

The class-free replacement for
``Lstr(translate=('serverResponses', text))`` (D38): V1-era servers
send English display text which we translate by exact lookup in the
legacy ``serverResponses`` corpus (missing translations pass the
text through unchanged, per the legacy convention). ``subs`` are
``('${TOKEN}', value)`` replacement pairs applied after
translation. The result is a verbatim value-form
:class:`~babase.LangStr`, so no further interpretation is applied
anywhere along the display path.

Exists only to serve V1-sourced flows; new server flows should send
display-final or LangStr forms per the lifetime rule instead (see
'Server-sent strings' in efrohome's asset-packages design doc).

functions.name: warm_up_string_measure
functions.doc:
warm_up_string_measure(string: str) -> None

Warm measurement of a string in the background.

Measuring OS-rendered text (foreign scripts, emoji, etc.) for the
first time can stall for tens of milliseconds on lazy OS font
loads. Code that will later need to measure such a string on the
logic thread (via get_string_width() or similar) can call this
ahead of time - when a window is built, for example - so that
cost is paid on a background thread and the later measure is a
cache hit. Returns immediately; nearly free for strings containing
no OS-rendered characters.

methods.name: on_construct_complete
methods.doc:
Called by construct-mode once required assets are in place.

Loads plugins, closes off subsystem registration, and finally
releases *intent* (the launch intent construct-mode has been
holding) to the app-mode that handles it.

Plugins load *here* -- rather than in the usual on_app_running
subsystem pass -- because this is the only spot where both of
the things they need are true at once:

* Every asset-package the meta-scan found a ``# ba_meta require
  asset-package`` line for is resolved and registered, so a
  plugin can load whatever it likes without tripping the
  too-early-load gate (see
  :func:`babase._asset_packages.check_asset_package_load`).
  That covers packages declared by plugins themselves, since the
  user scripts dir is scanned regardless of which plugins wind
  up enabled.
* No app-mode has been activated and no intent has been
  dispatched yet, so a plugin still gets to influence what
  happens next: replacing :attr:`mode_selector`, registering app
  subsystems, or driving its own intent via :meth:`set_intent`.

A happy side effect of deferring the *load* and not merely the
callback: a plugin's module is not imported until now either, so
no plugin-authored code at all -- module top-level included --
runs before assets are ready.

methods.name: on_control_permission_request

Ask the user whether something may control the app.

'Control' is deliberately broad: running commands, reading
this app's log, and whatever that grows into. Answer via

immediately (from policy).

The default answers ``CANNOT_ASK``, which is the honest
answer for a mode with no way to prompt -- the request is
then held and re-put once a mode that can ask activates.
An app-mode with a UI should override this; one running
without a user present (a dedicated server) should answer
``ALLOW``, since nobody is there to ask and the operator
already owns the account.

A deferred, language-agnostic complex string (native).

The verified-local counterpart of
:class:`bacommon.langstr.LangStrSpec` (see the D28 semantic
split -- holding one of these implies displayability here):
holds tokens, not text, and evaluates to a flat string in the
client's locale at display time. Construct from the canonical
wire JSON of any language-string form; pass the payload's
``packages`` manifest to bind integer-indexed values at parse,
and optionally a ``wrap`` triple (min-lines, max-lines,
max-chars-per-line; None = unlimited) as a usage-site override
of the string's definition-time line-wrapping. Immutable, with
content equality and hashing. Accepted anywhere
``str | babase.Lstr`` is accepted for display.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.doc:
evaluate(*, wrap: bool = True) -> str

Evaluate to flat display text in the client's locale.

Fail-visible: structural problems yield a ``LANGSTR_ERROR:...``
sentinel string (with a logged warning) rather than raising.

Pass ``wrap=False`` to skip the string's line-wrapping hints
(for code wrapping the text itself); newlines in the text are
kept either way.

methods.name: evaluate_timed
methods.doc:
evaluate_timed(*, wrap: bool = True) -> tuple[str, float | None]

Evaluate, also returning how soon the text changes.

Returns the text :meth:`evaluate` would (``wrap`` works the
same), plus the seconds until
it would next read differently -- a number only for time-varying
strings (those holding a moment, such as a countdown), else
``None``. Widgets showing a language-string handle this
themselves; this is for code displaying the text some other
way, which can re-evaluate when that time comes.

methods.name: from_text
methods.doc:
from_text(text: str) -> babase.LangStr

Wrap a plain string as a literal language-string.

The text is shown exactly as given in every locale -- any
``{`` or ``}`` displays literally, with no substitution. Use
this to pass a piece of already-final text (a name a mod
supplied, a value with no translation entry) through an API
that wants a :class:`~babase.LangStr`. Anything that needs
substitutions or translation should be an authored
asset-package entry instead, so its arguments are type-checked.

methods.name: join
methods.doc:
join(items: Sequence[babase.LangStr], separator: str = '') -> babase.LangStr

Combine language-strings into one, shown one after another.

``separator`` is literal text placed between items (a newline
for a list, say); its braces display literally. Each item keeps
its own translation and arguments, so a variable-length list
of authored entries (one line per player, ...) stays fully
localized. Items must be language-strings -- wrap plain text
with :meth:`from_text`. Raises ValueError for more than 256
items or a result nested too deeply.

Server code (or anything without a native language-string) can
build the same thing in spec form with
:meth:`bacommon.langstr.LangStrSpecValue.join`.

methods.name: to_json
methods.doc:
to_json() -> str

Return the canonical wire JSON for this language-string.

methods.name: to_resource_json
methods.doc:
to_resource_json() -> str

Return wire JSON for the self-describing resource-form
projection of this language-string (bound indexed nodes convert
via the native language tables). For persisting values beyond
their payload's package-index context. Raises ValueError for
unbound/unknown indexed nodes.

methods.name: on_app_mode_config
methods.doc:
Called when an app-mode is about to become active.

``config`` is the :class:`~babase.AppModeConfig` the incoming
mode built to describe how it should run; its concrete type
identifies the mode, so a plugin targeting a particular mode
checks for that mode's config type and amends what it finds::

    @override
    def on_app_mode_config(
        self, config: babase.AppModeConfig
    ) -> None:
        if isinstance(config, baclassic.ClassicAppModeConfig):
            config.ui_assets.trophy = my_trophy_texture

By convention, only *describe* here -- mutate the config and
touch nothing live. The mode reads the final result as it
activates, so if several plugins amend the same value the last
writer wins.

Only the config is passed, not the mode itself; that is
deliberate, to keep plugins amending the description rather
than reaching into a mode that is not active yet.

This never fires before construct-mode completes (plugins do
not run at all until then), so assets are safe to load here.

doc.__changed_from__: Called when the app reaches the running state.
doc.__modified_value__:
Called when the app reaches the running state.

Specifically, this fires once boot-time asset-package bring-up
has completed but before the launch intent is dispatched to an
app-mode. That means every asset-package the meta-scan found a
``# ba_meta require asset-package`` line for (including your
own) is resolved and safe to load by this point, while it is
still early enough to influence what the app does next --
setting :attr:`~babase.App.mode_selector`, registering app
subsystems, or driving an intent of your own via
:meth:`~babase.App.set_intent()`.

Note that a plugin's module is not even imported until this
point, so plugin code never runs before assets are ready.

doc.__changed_from__: Pauses updates to the root-ui while in existence.
doc.__modified_value__:
Pauses updates to the root-ui while in existence.

Instances are expected to be short-lived (covering an animation or
a server round-trip). Long holds get logged as warnings naming the
creation site; a common cause is an instance caught in a reference
cycle, where its release waits on the next explicit gc pass instead
of happening immediately (see :class:`~babase.GarbageCollectionSubsystem`).

classes.name: UIAssetSet
classes.doc:
The assets the ui_v1 widget layer draws itself with.

An app-mode that uses ui_v1 builds one of these (normally as
part of the config returned by its
:meth:`~babase.AppMode.new_app_mode_config`) and hands it to
:func:`bauiv1.set_ui_asset_set` when activating; this is what
lets an app-mode skin the ui. Supplying the art this way,
rather than ui_v1 reaching for it itself, is what keeps ui_v1
ignorant of which asset-packages the art lives in.

Slots hold asset *handles* (e.g.
:class:`~bauiv1.TextureHandle`), not loaded assets; nothing
loads until the set is applied at activation, so art that a
mode subclass or plugin replaces is never loaded at all.

Slots ui_v1 has no art of its own for are constructor
arguments, so a set is complete by construction. The rest
start out at ui_v1's own art. All slots are plain mutable
attributes, so an app-mode subclass or plugin amending a
config can restyle any of them before the set is applied.

methods.name: set_dormant
methods.doc:
Stop (or resume) counting as open while staying alive.

For states held somewhere that isn't actually showing anything,
such as a saved UI state waiting to be restored after a game.

methods.name: _describe_widget_context
methods.doc: Describe a live widget by its id and the window it is in.

doc.__changed_from__:
Checks to ensure a widget-owning object gets cleaned up properly.

This adds a check which will print an error message if the provided
object still exists ~5 seconds after the provided bauiv1.Widget
dies.

This is a good sanity check for any sort of object that wraps or
controls a bauiv1.Widget. For instance, a 'Window' class instance
has no reason to still exist once its root container bauiv1.Widget
has fully transitioned out and been destroyed. Circular references
or careless strong referencing can lead to such objects never
getting destroyed, however, and this helps detect such cases to
avoid memory leaks.
doc.__modified_value__:
Checks to ensure a widget-owning object gets cleaned up properly.

This adds a check which will log a warning (on the ``ba.ui``
logger) if the provided object still exists ~5 seconds after
the provided bauiv1.Widget dies.

This is a good sanity check for any sort of object that wraps or
controls a bauiv1.Widget. For instance, a 'Window' class instance
has no reason to still exist once its root container bauiv1.Widget
has fully transitioned out and been destroyed. Circular references
or careless strong referencing can lead to such objects never
getting destroyed, however, and this helps detect such cases to
avoid memory leaks.

The warning names where the object lived so it can be tracked
down from a log alone. By default that is derived from the
widget now, while it is alive: its id and the window it is in.
Pass ``context`` to override: a string, or a function taking
the object and returning one, called at warning time (windows
use this to describe their current state). Don't pass a bound
method or closure over the object; the check holds it strongly
and would itself keep the object alive.

methods.name: get_password
methods.doc:
Ask the user for a password.

Returns the entered password, or None if the user cancels or no
interactive UI is available (headless, etc.). Overridable
('virtual') so alternate UI layers can substitute their own
prompt; this default implementation shows a small
:class:`~bauiv1lib.passwordprompt.PasswordPromptWindow`.

Must be awaited on the logic thread. If the awaiting task is
cancelled, the prompt window is dismissed.

methods.name: on_app_mode_activated
methods.doc:
Called just after an app-mode becomes the active one.

Fires for every activation including the first, and always
after the mode's own :meth:`~babase.AppMode.on_activate`, so
the mode is fully in place by the time this runs. Useful for
work that needs *some* app-mode present but doesn't care
which -- e.g. re-putting a question that no earlier mode was
able to ask.

methods.name: request_main_window_recreate
methods.doc:
Rebuild the main window in place, whatever it is, soon.

The same rebuild a ui-scale or screen-size change triggers (its
state saved and restored, so a window lays itself out anew
without starting over), for when something else it is built
from has changed.

methods.name: suppress_window_recreates_while_alive
methods.doc:
Defer main-window auto-recreates for as long as a widget exists.

For ui living outside the main window but tied to it, such as a
popup menu opened from one of its buttons: a recreate replaces
the main window's widgets out from under it, leaving it wired to
dead ui. Deferred recreates run once the widget is gone,
including any out-transition.

classes.name: Viewer
classes.doc:
A live picture shown in ui; a little game scene, for instance.

A viewer is shown by a live depiction (a character viewer
depiction in a :func:`bauiv1.imagewidget`, say), which draws
its :attr:`source`, but belongs to no widget. Windows get torn down
and rebuilt all the time (on screen resizes, when navigating back
to them, ...) and what they were showing should carry on through
that instead of starting over, so viewers are kept by id in a
:class:`ViewerRegistry` and whatever shows one asks there first
for one to carry on with.

Subclass this to provide a particular sort of viewer.

:meta private:

methods.name: handle_drag
methods.doc:
A press passed to :meth:`handle_press` moved.

Where it is now, in the same fractions (and possibly outside
0-1, once dragged off the widget).

methods.name: handle_press
methods.doc:
A pointer pressed on a widget showing us.

Where, as fractions (0-1) across its width and up its height.

methods.name: handle_release
methods.doc: A press passed to :meth:`handle_press` let go.

methods.name: shutdown
methods.doc:
Stop for good and let go of everything we hold.

Called by the registry when we are retired; a viewer should
expect nothing further to be asked of it afterward.

methods.name: wants_presses
methods.doc:
Whether widgets showing us should pass along presses.

If so, they call :meth:`handle_press` and :meth:`handle_release`
(and take presses on them rather than letting them fall through
to whatever is beneath).

classes.name: ViewerRegistry
classes.doc:
Keeps viewers by id so they outlast the widgets showing them.

Viewers here are shut down once they have gone unshown for a short
while, and the number kept at once is small; asking for more
retires whichever has gone unshown the longest.

Access the single shared instance at ``bauiv1.app.ui_v1.viewers``.

:meta private:

methods.name: add
methods.doc:
Keep a viewer under an id.

Any viewer already kept under that id is shut down, as is
whichever viewer has gone unshown longest if we would
otherwise be keeping too many.

methods.name: clear
methods.doc: Shut down all viewers.

methods.name: get
methods.doc:
Return the viewer kept under an id, if there is one.

A viewer of some other type than the one asked for is treated
as not there (and will be replaced by whatever gets added).

methods.name: remove
methods.doc: Shut down the viewer kept under an id, if there is one.

Something that makes a picture for a live depiction to show.

These come from whatever provides such pictures (a scene viewer,
for instance) and are drawn by the depictions showing them.
They are made to outlast the widgets showing them, so a rebuilt
window can carry on showing what the old one was.

doc.__changed_from__:
Wrap a callable and arguments into a single callable object.

When passed a bound method as the callable, the instance portion of
it is weak-referenced, meaning the underlying instance is free to
die if all other references to it go away. Should this occur,
calling the weak-call is simply a no-op.

Think of this as a handy way to tell an object to do something at
some point in the future if it happens to still exist.

**EXAMPLE A:** This code will create a ``FooClass`` instance and
call its ``bar()`` method 5 seconds later; it will be kept alive
even though we overwrite its variable with None because the bound
method we pass as a timer callback (``foo.bar``) strong-references
it::

    foo = FooClass()
    babase.apptimer(5.0, foo.bar)
    foo = None

**EXAMPLE B:** This code will *not* keep our object alive; it will
die when we overwrite it with ``None`` and the timer will be a no-op
when it fires::

    foo = FooClass()
    babase.apptimer(5.0, ba.WeakCall(foo.bar))
    foo = None

**EXAMPLE C:** Wrap a method call with some positional and keyword
args::

    myweakcall = babase.WeakCall(self.dostuff, argval1,
                                 namedarg=argval2)

    # Now we have a single callable to run that whole mess.
    # The same as calling myobj.dostuff(argval1, namedarg=argval2)
    # (provided my_obj still exists; this will do nothing otherwise).
    myweakcall()

Note: additional args and keywords you provide to the weak-call
constructor are stored as regular stron

methods.name: get_scroll_state
methods.doc:
get_scroll_state() -> tuple[float, float, float] | None

For a scrolling widget, return (offset, content_extent,
visible_extent) along its scroll axis; None for other widgets.

The offset is in the widget's own terms, meaningful only to
:meth:`set_scroll_offset` on the same kind of widget. The extents
tell whether it still means the same thing: an offset saved from
one widget applies to another only if both extents match.

methods.name: get_slider_value
methods.doc:
get_slider_value() -> float | None

Returns a slider Widget's current value, or None if this is not a
slider.

Slider callbacks announce every change, so UI code can simply track
the value it is given; this exists for callers that would rather ask
the widget than shadow it -- automation and tests especially. Note
that callbacks are deferred to the end of the current UI operation,
so within one operation this reports the live value while a
callback-tracked copy may not have caught up yet.

doc.__changed_from__:
scroll_into_view() -> None

Scroll to show this widget if possible.
doc.__modified_value__:
scroll_into_view(animate: bool = True) -> None

Scroll to show this widget if possible.

Pass animate=False to snap straight to the destination instead of
gliding. Use that when the scrolled content was itself just built,
since there is then nothing on screen for the motion to read as
movement from.

methods.name: set_scroll_offset
methods.doc:
set_scroll_offset(offset: float) -> None

Jump a scrolling widget straight to an offset.

Takes an offset from :meth:`get_scroll_state`; clamped to the
content, with no glide and any inertia stopped. Raises TypeError
for widgets that don't scroll.

methods.name: autoretain
methods.doc:
Keep this actor alive without needing to hold a reference to it.

This keeps the actor in existence by storing a reference to it
with the :class:`~bascenev1.Activity` (or other
:class:`~bascenev1.ActorHost`) it was created in. The reference
is lazily released once :meth:`~bascenev1.Actor.exists()`
returns False for the actor or when the host is set as expired.
This can be a convenient alternative to storing references
explicitly just to keep an actor from dying. For convenience,
this method returns the actor it is called with, enabling
chained statements such as:
``myflag = bascenev1.Flag().autoretain()``

methods.name: exists
methods.doc:
Returns whether the actor is still present in a meaningful way.

Note that a dying character should still return True here as long as
their corpse is visible; this is about presence, not being 'alive'
(see :meth:`~bascenev1.Actor.is_alive()` for that).

If this returns False, it is assumed the actor can be completely
deleted without affecting the game; this call is often used when
pruning lists of actors, such as with
:meth:`bascenev1.Actor.autoretain()`

The default implementation of this method always return True.

Note that the boolean operator for the actor class calls this method,
so a simple ``if myactor`` test will conveniently do the right thing
even if myactor is set to None.

methods.name: getactivity
methods.doc:
Return the activity this actor is associated with.

If the activity no longer exists (or the actor was created in
a non-activity host such as a :class:`~bascenev1.LocalDisplay`),
raises a :class:`~bascenev1.ActivityNotFoundError` or returns
None depending on whether ``doraise`` is True.

methods.name: is_alive
methods.doc:
Returns whether the actor is 'alive'.

What this means is up to the actor. It is not a requirement for
actors to be able to die; just that they report whether they
consider themselves to be alive or not. In cases where
dead/alive is irrelevant, True should be returned.

methods.name: on_expire
methods.doc:
Called for remaining actors when their activity dies.

Actors can use this opportunity to clear callbacks or other
references which have the potential of keeping the
:class:`~bascenev1.Activity` alive inadvertently (activities can
not exit cleanly while any Python references to them remain.)

Once an actor is expired (see :attr:`~bascenev1.Actor.expired`)
it should no longer perform any game-affecting operations
(creating, modifying, or deleting nodes, media, timers, etc.)
Attempts to do so will likely result in errors.

methods.name: autoretain
methods.doc:
Keep this actor alive without needing to hold a reference to it.

This keeps the actor in existence by storing a reference to it
with the :class:`~bascenev1.Activity` (or other
:class:`~bascenev1.ActorHost`) it was created in. The reference
is lazily released once :meth:`~bascenev1.Actor.exists()`
returns False for the actor or when the host is set as expired.
This can be a convenient alternative to storing references
explicitly just to keep an actor from dying. For convenience,
this method returns the actor it is called with, enabling
chained statements such as:
``myflag = bascenev1.Flag().autoretain()``

methods.name: exists
methods.doc:
Returns whether the actor is still present in a meaningful way.

Note that a dying character should still return True here as long as
their corpse is visible; this is about presence, not being 'alive'
(see :meth:`~bascenev1.Actor.is_alive()` for that).

If this returns False, it is assumed the actor can be completely
deleted without affecting the game; this call is often used when
pruning lists of actors, such as with
:meth:`bascenev1.Actor.autoretain()`

The default implementation of this method always return True.

Note that the boolean operator for the actor class calls this method,
so a simple ``if myactor`` test will conveniently do the right thing
even if myactor is set to None.

methods.name: getactivity
methods.doc:
Return the activity this actor is associated with.

If the activity no longer exists (or the actor was created in
a non-activity host such as a :class:`~bascenev1.LocalDisplay`),
raises a :class:`~bascenev1.ActivityNotFoundError` or returns
None depending on whether ``doraise`` is True.

methods.name: is_alive
methods.doc:
Returns whether the actor is 'alive'.

What this means is up to the actor. It is not a requirement for
actors to be able to die; just that they report whether they
consider themselves to be alive or not. In cases where
dead/alive is irrelevant, True should be returned.

methods.name: on_expire
methods.doc:
Called for remaining actors when their activity dies.

Actors can use this opportunity to clear callbacks or other
references which have the potential of keeping the
:class:`~bascenev1.Activity` alive inadvertently (activities can
not exit cleanly while any Python references to them remain.)

Once an actor is expired (see :attr:`~bascenev1.Actor.expired`)
it should no longer perform any game-affecting operations
(creating, modifying, or deleting nodes, media, timers, etc.)
Attempts to do so will likely result in errors.

This keeps the actor in existence by storing a reference to it
with the :class:`~bascenev1.Activity` (or other

methods.name: exists
methods.doc:
Returns whether the actor is still present in a meaningful way.

Note that a dying character should still return True here as long as
their corpse is visible; this is about presence, not being 'alive'
(see :meth:`~bascenev1.Actor.is_alive()` for that).

deleted without affecting the game; this call is often used when
pruning lists of actors, such as with
:meth:`bascenev1.Actor.autoretain()`

The default implementation of this method always return True.

Note that the boolean operator for the actor class calls this method,
so a simple ``if myactor`` test will conveniently do the right thing
even if myactor is set to None.

constants.name: CATEGORY_ALIASES
constants.doc:
dict() -> new empty dictionary
dict(mapping) -> new dictionary initialized from a mapping object's
    (key, value) pairs
dict(iterable) -> new dictionary initialized as if via:
    d = {}
    for k, v in iterable:

constants.doc:
str(object='') -> str
str(bytes_or_buffer[, encoding[, errors]]) -> str

Create a new string object from the given object. If encoding or
errors is specified, then the object must expose a data buffer
that will be decoded using the given encoding and error handler.
Otherwise, returns the result of object.__str__() (if defined)
or repr(object).
encoding defaults to 'utf-8'.
errors defaults to 'strict'.
